facts.text: My bottom half was the launch pad Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin lifted off from. It still sits at 0.67416 N, 23.47314 E, a spot found in Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter images.

Next to me the crew left a panel of 100 small mirrors. Scientists still bounce lasers off Apollo mirrors, and that is how we know the Earth and Moon drift apart about 3.8 cm a year, about as fast as your fingernails grow.

Buzz Aldrin reported the flag was blown over by my engine blast when the crew took off. Years later, NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter camera found flags still standing at every Apollo site except mine.

My top half, the part that flew the crew back up, was set loose in lunar orbit. NASA does not know what happened to it. The guess at the time was that it crashed into the Moon within one to four months.

facts.text: When I landed, shiny rocks confused my radar, my engine did not shut off, and I bounced off the Moon twice, once as high as 10 meters.
I dug four trenches by remote control and showed the lunar soil was like wet sand, solid enough to hold an Apollo lunar module.
About two and a half years after I landed, Apollo 12 set down about 180 meters away. Pete Conrad and Alan Bean walked over to me and took parts home, including my soil scoop and camera.
I launched from Cape Canaveral, Florida, Launch Complex 36B.
About 10 kg of my 296 kg went back to Earth. The rest of me is still in the Ocean of Storms.

'Feels like the one robot people came back to visit': no NASA page states it is the only one; keep as feeling, never as a claim.

facts.text: Five Apollo crews, on Apollo 12, 14, 15, 16 and 17, set up stations like us. We carried seismometers to feel moonquakes, and each station ran on a small nuclear generator fueled with plutonium.
Most of us were still working well when the money for our support ran out. NASA shut our experiments down on September 30, 1977.
Our experiments were switched off, but our radios kept sending a plain signal. JPL and others used it to study the Moon's position and to help navigate spacecraft.
We were built to last one year. We worked for up to 8 years, and scientists sent us more than 153,000 commands.

facts.text: I am one of three electric moon buggies driven on the Moon, on Apollo 15, 16 and 17. John Young parked me 300 feet east of the lander so my TV camera could watch the crew lift off.
On our second drive, John Young's suit caught on my right rear fender and tore it off, so the dust got worse on every drive after.
Before we left, astronaut Charlie Duke laid a photo of his family on the Moon. It is still there.
Going down a 15-degree slope I hit 10.6 miles per hour, a new speed record on the Moon.

facts.text: I was built for 90 Martian days and kept going 60 times longer. I drove 45.16 km, a record on another world until Perseverance passed me in 2026.
My twin and I confirmed that water stood on the surface of Mars for a long time in ancient times.
A dust storm that covered the whole planet blocked the sunlight my solar panels needed. My last signal reached Earth on June 10, 2018.
NASA sent me more than a thousand commands to wake me up before ending my mission on February 13, 2019.
I was the first to drive a full marathon on another world, 42.195 km.

facts.text: I landed in Gusev Crater, a possible former lake, and drove 7.7 km.
On May 1, 2009 I got stuck in soft soil at a spot called Troy. Engineers used test rovers on Earth to plan my escape, but by late January 2010 NASA made me a parked science station instead.
I was planned for 90 Martian days. I worked for six years, two months and 19 days, more than 25 times longer.
Stuck in place, I could not tilt my solar panels toward the winter Sun. My last call home was March 22, 2010.
My name came from 9-year-old Sofi Collis, who once lived in an orphanage. Her essay beat nearly 10,000 others: 'Thank you for the Spirit and the Opportunity.'

facts.text: I weigh 10.6 kg, about 23 pounds, and I am about 30 centimeters tall when I stand up.
My lander bounced like a giant beach ball about 15 times, as high as 50 feet.
I was planned for one week and lasted 83 days, 12 times longer.
I am named after civil-rights hero Sojourner Truth. A 12-year-old student, Valerie Ambroise, picked my name. My lander was named the Carl Sagan Memorial Station.
I live in Ares Vallis, an ancient flood plain. Our final data reached Earth on September 27, 1997.

facts.text: I made the first truly successful landing on Mars, on July 20, 1976.
On July 28, 1976, my robot arm scooped up the first soil samples and fed them to my biology lab to look for signs of life. I also sent weather reports, daily and later weekly.

In November 1982, a command from Earth about my battery charging accidentally overwrote the numbers my antenna used to point at Earth. Contact was lost and never came back. It was not Mars that ended my mission; it was a faulty command.
I was renamed the Thomas Mutch Memorial Station, after the leader of my camera team.

facts.text: An orbiter photographed me hanging from my parachute. It was the first time one spacecraft photographed another landing on a planet.
I dug a trench and found bright clumps that vanished four days later. That is what ice does on Mars.
On July 31, 2008, NASA officially announced there is water on Mars, based on a sample I collected and heated in my tiny ovens.
I found perchlorate salts, which made scientists look again at the old Viking data.
As the arctic summer ended, I had less and less sunlight for power. My last signal reached Earth on November 2, 2008.

facts.text: My arm set a seismometer on the ground. I was the first to detect marsquakes, 1,319 of them, and they showed scientists the crust, mantle and core of Mars.
On December 1, 2018, my sensors caught a low rumble from the vibrations of the Martian wind, blowing about 10 to 15 miles per hour.
Dust slowly covered my solar panels until my batteries ran out. My last call home was December 15, 2022.
Scientists are still making discoveries from my marsquake data.
I live in Elysium Planitia, named for the paradise of the afterlife in Greek myth.

facts.text: I was designed for no more than five test flights in 30 days. I flew 72 times across nearly three years.
On January 18, 2024, my rotor blades broke when I landed on flight 72. I can't fly anymore.

My first flight, on April 19, 2021, was the first powered, controlled flight on another planet. It has been called a 'Wright Brothers moment', and I carry a swatch of cloth from the real Wright Flyer.
On my last flight, my navigation camera could not find enough features to track over the smooth sand ripples, so I came down too fast and sideways.
